title: Highly classified US national security communications network goes down
titleZh: Highly classified US national security communications network goes down
author: monkeydust
relevanceReason: 命中 1 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter. The NSA closed its campus to most employees on Tuesday night, reverting to essential personnel only as it works to restore the network, according to a voicemail inbox used by NSA employees and a source familiar with the matter.

The move to further restrict staffing levels came just hours after the NSA told employees they could return to work as normal. It is not clear what prompted the reversal. The agency had staggered employee arrivals earlier in the day as it worked to address the issue.
The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said.

“The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.”
A source familiar with the matter told CNN that restoration of the network was ongoing but not yet complete.

children.author: derangedHorse
children.textRawHtml:
I saw a post claiming the issues we're seeing is a result of hasty fixes to AI-discovered vulnerabilities. This seems like the most plausible reason for all of this to me.

Doubly so when we consider companies with external security audits. Those external security firms sometimes have access to better models and larger budgets than the developers responsible for fixing the vulnerabilities they uncover.

children.author: Iolaum
children.textRawHtml: Are they doing manual fixes? I have trouble imagining someone who knows how to code and leverages AI properly is breaking something in the process of fixing it. Unless my two assumptions on the people working on this thing are wrong.

children.author: lancebeet
children.textRawHtml: Since agents got really at this, I've used them to uncover quite a few verifiable vulnerabilities. Some were easily patchable oversights, but others uncovered flawed architectural decisions which required significant rewrites to fix (done with agents, of course), with a non-zero probability of regressions. I guess your assumption here depends on your definitions of "knowing how to code" and "leveraging AI properly" but it's definitely possible for someone with years of professional experience as a software developer, using the best AI tools on the market, to unintentionally break something when they fix something else.

children.author: anavat
children.textRawHtml: These are huge systems with multiple application, data, and network layers. You can QA the app to death and make sure it works locally and on staging, but then you have firewalls, load balancers, access policies, replication, VPCs, and whatnot. And CloudFormation templates (or whatever IaC you have) is of little help because they are out of sync because someone has definitely made some manual changes in the load balancer config a year go while fighting another crisis.

children.author: IanCal
children.textRawHtml:
Deploys have always carried risks, and the speed and checking has always had to be balanced against the benefits of/risks of not deploying now.

You may also have fixed the issue but had a bug in some part of your deployment.

And the more core the bug is (issue in an os) I would wager the larger the set of services you’re likely to need to update is.

comments.author: usernomdeguerre
comments.textRawHtml:
People seem to be leaning on the AI speculation from the "vibe coded" angle, but couldn't this also be an "AI is the reason" from the attacker side? I think we've seen more than a fair share of AI assisted exploits that chain many small vulnerabilities into something more pronounced. I'm thinking of the rash of attacks in SK and China against Banks using offensive harnesses.

I'd be more willing to believe the network in question here was under an attack load that either was probed or exploited far enough that shutting it down was worthwhile. It seems more reasonable to me than believing they've let AI run amok on their internals such that it's now failing.

Not because I'm deifying the NSA but because the system has to be decades old, at least, and I wouldn't expect significant changes to something that "just works".
